title: Generics
summary: Write classes and methods that work for any element type while staying type-safe: type parameters, bounded types, extends and super wildcards, and the limits of type erasure.
introduction: You have used generics every time you wrote List<String>: the angle brackets tell the compiler what the list holds, so it rejects a wrong element at compile time and hands back the right type without a cast. This lesson shows how to write that kind of code yourself. You build a generic Box class, write generic methods, constrain a type parameter with a bound so you can compare elements, use wildcards to accept whole families of lists, and learn which things generics cannot do because the type information is erased at run time.
learningObjectives: Explain what generics fix compared with raw types and casts
Declare a generic class and a generic method with a type parameter
Constrain a type parameter with extends and use extends and super wildcards
Recognise the limits imposed by type erasure

blocks.text: Before Java 5 a list held `Object` values. Anything could be added, every read needed a cast, and a wrong element surfaced only at run time as a `ClassCastException`, often far from the line that caused it. **Raw types** still compile today for backwards compatibility, but the compiler warns you, and the warning is worth taking seriously.

blocks.text: With `List<String>` the `names.add(42)` line does not compile, `get` returns a `String`, and the cast disappears. Generics move the check from the user of the program to the compiler, which is always the cheaper place to find a bug.

A **type parameter** in angle brackets after the class name stands for a type that the user of the class chooses. Inside the class `T` is used like any type: for fields, parameters and return values. By convention type parameters are single capital letters: `T` for a type, `E` for an element, `K` and `V` for a key and a value.

blocks.title: Box.java

blocks.text: `Box<String>` and `Box<Integer>` are two uses of the same class, each checked separately: `words.put(42)` would be a compile error. The empty diamond `<>` on the right-hand side tells the compiler to copy the type argument from the declaration.

A single method can have its own type parameter, declared in angle brackets **before the return type**. The compiler infers `T` from the arguments at each call. When the method needs to do something with the elements beyond passing them around, it needs a **bound**: `<T extends Comparable<T>>` promises that every `T` has a `compareTo` method, which is exactly what `max` needs.

blocks.title: Utils.java

blocks.text: `max` works for `Integer`, `String`, `LocalDate` and any class that implements `Comparable`, and it refuses at compile time a list of a class that does not. Without the bound, `item.compareTo(best)` would not compile, because a plain `T` is only known to be an `Object`.

Generics are **invariant**: a `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`, even though an `Integer` is a `Number`, because otherwise a method holding the `List<Number>` view could add a `Double` into a list of integers. Wildcards relax this where it is safe. `List<? extends Number>` accepts a list of any subtype of `Number` and lets you **read** elements as `Number`; `List<? super Integer>` accepts a list of `Integer` or any supertype and lets you **write** integers into it. The memory aid is PECS: producer `extends`, consumer `super`.

blocks.title: Totals.java

blocks.text: Java implements generics by **type erasure**: after compilation a `Box<String>` is just a `Box`, and the type argument is gone. That design kept old code working, but it rules out a few things you may expect from other languages.

items: Type arguments must be reference types: `List<int>` is an error; use `List<Integer>`.
You cannot write `new T()` or `new T[10]`, because at run time nobody knows what `T` was.
`obj instanceof List<String>` cannot be checked; only `instanceof List<?>` is allowed.
A static field cannot have type `T`, since static members are shared by all `Box<...>` uses.
Assigning between different type arguments is an error, which is the invariance rule from above.

blocks.title: Invariance.java
javac Invariance.java
blocks.content:
Invariance.java:7: error: incompatible types: List<String> cannot be converted to List<Object>
        List<Object> anything = names;
                                ^
1 error

blocks.text: The compiler is right to refuse: if line 7 were allowed, line 8 would place an `Integer` into a list that `names` still believes holds only strings. When you need a method that accepts lists of anything, use `List<?>` or a wildcard bound instead of `List<Object>`.

blocks.title: Primitives are not type arguments
blocks.text: `List<int> numbers = new ArrayList<>();` fails with `error: unexpected type` followed by `required: reference` and `found: int`. Use the wrapper class, `List<Integer>`, and let autoboxing convert values on the way in and out. The same applies to `Map<String, double>`: write `Map<String, Double>`.

blocks.title: How much to write yourself
blocks.text: Most day-to-day Java uses generics rather than defines them: you will declare `List<Order>` far more often than `class Repository<T>`. Write a generic class when you catch yourself copying a container or utility for a second element type, and keep its type parameters few and well named.

questions.question: Because `String` extends `Object`, a `List<String>` can be assigned to a variable of type `List<Object>`.
questions.explanation: Generic types are invariant. Allowing the assignment would let code add any `Object` to a list that other code treats as strings.

questions.question: Which declaration is valid Java?
questions.explanation: Type arguments must be reference types, so the wrapper class `Integer` is used; `int`, `integer` and `Int` are not accepted.
